title: Less Code, More Context: How AI Is Reshaping the Developer Role
summary: As a developer delegates more work to AI, where does their expertise matter most? Experts share how they see the role shifting.
body_markdown:
Software development is not the first profession to be reshaped by a new tool.


SAP TechEd in 2026: The Autonomous Enterprise Becomes a Reality


[Read the innovation news guide](https://www.sap.com/topics/events/teched/innovation-news-guide-2026)


Spreadsheets enabled accountants to automate calculations, digital tools let film editors rearrange scenes without physically cutting and splicing film, and architectural software simplified the drawing of plans.


However, these tools did not remove the need to understand the goal, exercise professional judgment, and evaluate the result.


AI is introducing a comparable shift for developers: from carrying out every implementation step themselves toward defining requirements, shaping solutions, and validating outcomes.


As developers delegate more work to AI, where does their expertise matter most? We asked developers in the SAP community and speakers at[SAP TechEd in 2026](https://news.sap.com/topics/sap-teched/) how they see the shift.


## **Context matters**


“Business context is more important than ever,” said Douglas Cezar Kuchler, SAP champion, SAP Solution Architecture, sovanta AG.


That means looking beyond the immediate task, according to Simon Coen, lead for SAP Cloud Technologies at j&s-soft AG: “You really need to understand the business processes involved and how the solution fits into the existing system landscape.”


Indeed, in[interviews with 22 advanced AI users](https://github.blog/news-insights/octoverse/the-new-identity-of-a-developer-what-changes-and-what-doesnt-in-the-ai-era/) , GitHub found that developers see themselves less as “code producers” and more as “creative directors of code,” with the core skill shifting from implementation to orchestration and verification. Developers must think at the level of outcomes and systems, not snippets.


Dr. Eng. Tomasz Wilk, GDC Poland PBS SAP chief architect, said he already sees the change in his daily work: “I spend much less time on coding itself and much more time talking to customers, understanding their needs, defining requirements, testing, and validating results.”


There is also a change in what developers need to specify. “We are no longer primarily specifying classes, methods, or individual pieces of code. We are describing a use case, a step in a business process, or ultimately a business capability,” Wilk said. “We become less the implementer and more the person responsible for expressing the business intent clearly enough for AI to turn it into a working solution.”


AI can[amplify an organization’s existing strengths and weaknesses](https://dora.dev/research/2025/dora-report/) . Without a clear understanding of users and their needs, accelerated code generation risks simply taking a team in the wrong direction faster.


Kuchler believes the business objective, not the requested output, should shape the solution.


Imagine a customer request for an order-monitoring report. AI could help deliver the report quickly. But understanding why the customer wants it might uncover a different opportunity: anticipating delivery risks and preventing customer dissatisfaction. For example, the developer could explore an architecture in which an AI agent accesses relevant SAP business data via a governed ABAP RAP service and uses predictive capabilities, such as SAP-RPT, to identify potential delivery risks.


“That requires understanding AI capabilities, enterprise agent architecture, business value and processes, data relationships, desired outcomes, and decision boundaries before designing the solution,” Kuchler said. “AI can help us build what we ask for. Understanding the business helps us discover what is actually worth building.”


The importance of business context isn’t new, but now AI needs it to be made explicit. Andrei Liakhavets, SAP developer at BeNeering, observed: “In the past, a lot of business context was not documented in any way, but directly translated from words into code.” With AI, he added, “that ‘documenting’ step is less avoidable.”


For Wilk, capturing business intent also matters when a solution needs to be migrated, regenerated, or redesigned. “If the original business intent and context were never captured precisely, we may reproduce the functionality but lose the reasoning behind it,” he said. “The new solution may look correct and still behave differently where it matters. The more implementation we delegate to AI, the more precisely we need to preserve the intent behind it.”


## **Design: turning context into a solution**


Kuchler said AI is changing how developers divide their attention among business understanding, design, and implementation: “AI is changing the balance: we can increasingly guide implementation while concentrating on defining the right solution, its constraints and authorizations, and how to validate the results.”


Coen described the same shift: “The role of a developer is shifting more and more to defining problems, making architectural decisions, guiding, and evaluating rather than implementing.”


That means translating business understanding into both architectural decisions and implementation guidance. Sergio Guerrero, principal at Shockwave Consulting LLC, described combining business context and rules with technical instructions covering SAP Fiori best practices, CDS modeling, OData, and the application being built. That requires a view beyond individual generated components.


“Being able to understand a solution as a whole, rather than just small pieces of code, is fundamental while collaborating with AI tools,” Guerrero explained. “There was already a design step before AI. Now, designing has become more important.”


“At the same time, I do not think everything has to be perfectly defined upfront,” Wilk said. “AI can actually help us with the discovery itself.” Prototypes don’t need to offer any answer; they can “help the customer understand the problem better, challenge initial assumptions, and discover what they actually need.”


For Wilk, AI-first doesn’t mean approaching problems with “Where can we put an agent?” but rather with the problem in mind, then asking whether AI is the right solution.


## **Still building, still responsible**


However, not every developer sees this as a shift from building to designing. Liakhavets sees it differently: “I do not like such wording. For me, designing is something theoretical, and building is the practical part. And with AI or without AI, it is still building. So, for me it is still building, just with a new tool.”


What hasn’t changed is responsibility. “You still need to understand what AI is doing, as you are responsible for its results,” Liakhavets said.


This responsibility extends through validation. “Developers need to connect business objectives with AI capabilities, design interactions between agents and enterprise systems, establish constraints and authorizations, and evaluate the quality and trustworthiness of outcomes,” Kuchler said.


For Coen, technical expertise remains essential: “You have to be able to challenge the outcome of the AI rather than simply accepting what was generated.” Business context helps define the right solution; engineering judgement helps establish whether AI has actually delivered it.


## **Work is changing, not value**


AI is changing how developers build, but not what makes their work valuable. Understanding the business helps them identify the right problem, clear intent guides implementation, and technical judgment determines whether the result is fit for purpose. Context needs to guide the work through to validation.


The measure of success is not how much code AI can produce, but whether the resulting solution serves the business.


As Kuchler put it: “I’m becoming less focused on how much code I can produce, and much more interested in how much business value I can help create through software.”
